name: THE 28 MAIZE LATER BURGER (comes with corn salsa)

recipe.history:
Maize — Zea mays — is the great agricultural achievement of the Americas, a crop that did not exist in the Old World before 1492 and yet became one of the three most important staple grains in the world within two centuries of contact. It was domesticated from its wild ancestor teosinte by Indigenous peoples in the Balsas River valley of what is now southwest Mexico approximately nine thousand years ago, a transformation so dramatic — from a grass with a few kernels to a cob with hundreds — that it required millennia of selective cultivation and was for a long time considered the single most significant act of artificial selection in human history. Maize fed the Olmec, the Maya, the Aztec, the Inca, and the agricultural civilizations of the North American plains, and it was the spiritual center of Mesoamerican cosmology: the Popol Vuh, the Mayan creation epic, describes human beings as made from corn. Corn salsa — fresh corn kernels cut from the cob, combined with tomatoes, onions, cilantro, jalapeño, and lime — is a Tex-Mex preparation that captures the sweetness and crunch of summer corn in a form that is more condiment than side dish.

Corn arrived on American burgers as a topping most visibly through the Southwest and California fusion movements of the 1990s, when chefs who had grown up eating elote (grilled Mexican corn with cotija and chile) began importing that flavor profile into their cooking. Corn salsa specifically became a burger topping through the Tex-Mex fast-casual chains that spread across the country in the 2000s, where its freshness and color provided a visual and textural contrast to the standard lettuce-tomato-onion formula. The natural sweetness of fresh corn plays off the savory depth of beef in a way that is both surprising and immediately intuitive, and the jalapeño and lime in the salsa provide the heat and acid that balance the corn's sugar. On a summer burger with fresh ears at peak sweetness, the corn salsa needs nothing to improve it — it is already nearly perfect.

Some of my most contented kitchen hours have been spent at a cutting board in late July, shucking corn. There is something about the act — the resistance of the husk, the silk coming away in soft threads, the sudden freshness of the corn smell — that feels like a seasonal ritual, a thing you do because the season demands it. I learned to make corn salsa from a recipe on the back of a chip bag that I have since lost and never been able to find again. The proportions I use now are my own: more jalapeño than most people would recommend, more lime than seems polite, less tomato, and the corn cut from the cob rather than canned, always. I charred the corn in a cast-iron skillet once on a whim and discovered that five minutes of dry heat on a corn kernel produces a nutty, slightly smoky depth that no amount of lime or cilantro can replicate — and I have never made corn salsa from raw kernels again.

The medium rare standard — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — matters especially with a corn salsa burger because the salsa is cold and the contrast is the point. The warm, pink, yielding patty against the chilled crunch of the salsa creates a temperature and texture interplay that is one of the burger world's great sensory pleasures. A well-done patty would be merely a warm platform for the salsa — it would not contribute its own character to the experience. Medium rare means the beef is still an active participant in the dish, its residual warmth slightly taking the chill off the salsa where they meet at the surface while the interior of each component stays distinct. This is cooking as composition, not just as preparation.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 medium red bell pepper, finely diced
1 small ripe tomato, seeded and finely diced
2 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce, minced
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
1 head romaine lettuce, inner leaves only
instructions: 1. Make the charred corn salsa (at least 30 minutes ahead): Heat a dry cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Place husked corn cobs directly in the pan and char, turning every 2–3 minutes, until the kernels are deeply golden to black in spots on all sides, about 10–12 minutes total. Remove and cool until handleable. Stand each cob upright and cut the kernels from the cob with a sharp knife.

2. Combine charred corn kernels, diced red bell pepper, red onion, jalapeño, tomato, and cilantro in a bowl. Add lime juice, olive oil, ground cumin, smoked paprika, and kosher salt. Toss to combine. Let sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes for the flavors to meld. Taste and adjust seasoning before serving.

3. Make the chipotle mayo: Whisk egg yolks and Dijon mustard in a medium bowl until slightly pale. Add neutral oil drop by drop while whisking constantly until about a quarter of the oil has been incorporated and the emulsion is established. Then add the remaining oil in a thin, steady stream, whisking continuously. Fold in minced chipotle peppers, adobo sauce, and lime juice. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warm milk, mix on low for 2 minutes, then knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

5. Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g, shape into tight balls, and proof on parchment-lined baking sheets covered for 45 minutes.
6. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Form the beef patties: Divide ground beef into 6 equal portions of 150g. Handle minimally. Form each into a 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patty with a thumb indent. Season both sides with salt and cracked pepper immediately before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties dry and undisturbed for 3 minutes. Flip once. Place a slice of Monterey Jack on each patty. Cook for 2–2.5 more minutes. Confirm internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
9. Slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a buttered skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.

10. Assemble each burger: Spread chipotle mayo generously on both cut faces of the bun. Place romaine leaves and tomato slices on the bottom bun. Add avocado slices. Set the rested Monterey Jack-topped patty on top. Spoon a generous portion of charred corn salsa over the patty. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve with extra corn salsa on the side.
